headline: Garbage burning poses health hazard in Palampur, Himachal Pradesh
content: Large-scale burning of garbage at the waste treatment plant of the Palampur Municipal Corporation has become a serious health hazard for residents living nearby. Despite repeated directions from the State Pollution Control Board (SPCB) against the practice, garbage is allegedly being set on fire continuously, releasing thick smoke and potentially harmful fumes into the surrounding areas.Incidents of garbage burning have also been reported at other places in the city. Municipal Corporation employees themselves are allegedly burning waste instead of ensuring its scientific disposal. Near Hotel T Bud, burning is reportedly a regular practice and photographs of the site show the extent of the problem and raise questions about the enforcement of environmental regulations by the civic authorities.Residents say senior corporation officials are well aware of the situation, but no effective measures have been taken to stop recurring incidents. Those living around the plant and in other affected localities have expressed concern over deteriorating air quality and the health risks of continuous exposure to smoke from burning waste.A Municipal Corporation official claimed that the fire at the treatment plant was accidental. He said the staff there had been told not to set garbage on fire and that such incidents should not recur.Local MLA Ashish Butail said he had received reports of garbage burning at the plant and assured that action would be taken against those responsible. He termed garbage burning a serious offence, prohibited under National Green Tribunal (NGT) directions and the regulations of the Himachal Pradesh State Pollution Control Board.The issue is not new. In 2022, the Himachal Pradesh High Court had taken cognisance of fires at the Palampur corporation’s garbage treatment plant and issued notices to various departments and agencies, including the Municipal Corporation, the State Pollution Control Board and the Town and Country Planning Department. Despite this and the directions of the pollution control authorities, garbage burning continues.Residents are demanding immediate intervention by the Pollution Control Board and the district administration, strict action against those responsible and an end to the open burning of municipal waste in Palampur.

headline: AAP accuses Congress of betraying people of Himachal | Hindustan Times
content: Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) leader Manish Sisodia on Friday accused the Congress government in Himachal Pradesh of betraying the people by failing to fulfil its pre-poll promises.Addressing a press conference in Dharamshala, Sisodia said, “People of Himachal Pradesh trusted Congress and voted it to power, but the party has gone back on its promises. Women and daughters of the state today feel cheated and betrayed.”On Delhi’s pollution crisis, Sisodia said air pollution was not confined to Delhi’s borders and required a coordinated effort by the Centre and all northern states. He said dust and pollution did not recognise state boundaries and called for a joint strategy involving Delhi, Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and other northern states.He also urged authorities to stop blaming farmers for pollution, arguing that construction activities, vehicles and other sources also contributed to the problem. “It is a collective failure of north India, and the Centre must work with all northern states to find a solution,” he said.On the rising drug menace in Punjab, Sisodia rejected allegations that drug abuse had reached its peak in the state. He claimed that the Bhagwant Mann government had dismantled the political patronage system supporting drug trafficking and arrested around 90,000 drug smugglers.He alleged that previous Akali-BJP and Congress governments had allowed drug networks to operate with political support. He also accused the BJP of failing to prevent drug trafficking through Gujarat’s ports.

headline: Himachal clears green cess on goods sent out of state
content: Dharamshala: The Himachal Pradesh assembly passed seven bills on Friday amid objections from the BJP to three legislations concerning the proposed environmental cess on goods transported by road, promotions of govt employees and technical universities in the state.The Himachal Pradesh (Carriage of Certain Goods by Road) Taxation Amendment Bill, 2026, provides for an environmental cess of up to Rs 25 per tonne on specified goods transported by road out of the state. It was passed by a voice vote. Chief minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu clarified that Rs 25 was the maximum permissible rate and govt could decide to levy Rs 1, Rs 2 or Rs 3 per tonne. He assured the House that the cess would not be imposed on transporters or construction materials such as sand and gravel.Leader of opposition Jai Ram Thakur argued that roads were the only means of transportation in the hill state and any additional levy would ultimately burden consumers and the poor.BJP MLAs Randhir Sharma and Trilok Jamwal also urged the govt to withdraw the legislation, arguing that the additional cess would increase the cost of essential commodities and construction materials. Jamwal said households were already paying such a cess through electricity bills.Defending the legislation, the CM cited the example of clinker produced in Himachal and transported to cement factories outside the state, where cement manufactured using the state’s resources was sold cheaper than in Himachal.The Government Services (Regulation of Qualifying Experience and Promotion) Bill, 2026, also faced opposition from the BJP, with Thakur accusing the Congress govt of attempting to deny contractual employees their legitimate service benefits.Sukhu said it was intended to protect the interests of both contractual and regular employees.The other five bills passed by the House were the Himachal Pradesh Sukhashray (Social Security of Women and Children of the State) Bill, the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement (Himachal Pradesh Amendment) Bill, the Himachal Pradesh Land Revenue (Amendment) Bill, the Himachal Pradesh Panchayati Raj (Third Amendment) Bill and the Himachal Pradesh Technical Universities (Amendment) Bill, 2026.

headline: Adamant over Himachal minister’s dismissal, BJP stages walkout
content: Adamant about the dismissal of Revenue Minister Jagat Singh Negi, the opposition BJP on Friday staged a walkout of the Himachal Pradesh legislative assembly in Dharamshala.On the fifth day of the winter session, heated exchanges erupted as the BJP launched an offensive against the government over Negi’s remarks regarding the Indian Army on Wednesday.As proceedings began, Leader of the Opposition Jairam Thakur raised the issue, saying that a senior minister had made serious remarks concerning the Army and ‘Operation Sindoor’.Pressing for a public apology by Negi and his dismissal from the Cabinet.

headline: ‘Himachal on sale’? Sukhu turns charge on BJP
content: Dharamshala: Himachal Pradesh chief minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu on Friday said no state assets, including Peterhoff in Shimla, would be sold, while accusing the BJP of “selling Himachal” during its previous term.Replying to the adjournment motion under Rule 67, brought by the Opposition BJP on Tuesday and titled ‘Himachal on sale’, Sukhu clarified the govt’s position on Peterhoff, saying the existing structure would be dismantled and more than 100 rooms constructed at the site. He said the tender for dismantling the building would be opened on Nov 27.The CM said 30 rooms were similarly being built at the under-construction Dwarka Niketan in Delhi.Sukhu also announced strict action against benami land purchases near Gaggal airport, while accusing the previous BJP govt of allotting thousands of bighas of industrial land in Baddi-Nalagarh to private companies at throwaway prices.Targeting the BJP, Sukhu alleged that nearly 4,000 to 5,000 bighas of land in the Baddi-Nalagarh industrial belt had been allotted to industrialists at Re 1 per square metre under customised packages during its previous term.The CM alleged that these concessions could eventually facilitate real estate dealings rather than industrial activity.He also alleged that the previous govt had waived stamp duty worth hundreds of crores of rupees on these land allotments. While big industrial houses received land at nominal rates, Himachali entrepreneurs had to purchase industrial plots at market prices and pay stamp duty, he said.Highlighting the Wildflower Hall case, Sukhu said the govt had recovered Rs 401 crore, including interest calculated over 23 years, from the private operator. The property was subsequently auctioned and, under the new arrangement, the state would receive a minimum annual guarantee of Rs 35-40 crore even if the hotel remained closed.On the state’s financial position, Sukhu said Himachal Pradesh would receive Rs 20,000 crore in BBMB arrears over the next 20 years, crediting his govt’s efforts with securing the dues. He also said the withdrawal of the revenue deficit grant had deprived the state of Rs 8,000 crore, but assured govt employees that salaries and pensions would not be stopped. Pension arrears would be cleared gradually, he added.The chief minister further announced plans to procure 1,000 additional electric buses within the next six months. The move was aimed at making HRTC financially self-reliant while reducing pollution, he said.Sukhu also alleged that a company that had received a project near Manali was a defaulter in Uttarakhand at the time of the allotment. Around 124 bighas of land, valued at more than Rs 500 crore, had been allotted to the company by the previous BJP govt, he claimed.Defending his govt’s decisions, Sukhu said it was committed to protecting the state’s assets and making Himachal financially self-reliant. He accused the BJP of staging a walkout because it did not want to hear the govt’s response to the allegations. The chief minister urged the Speaker to reject the motion. The Speaker subsequently rejected the adjournment motion.

headline: You searched for " himachal pradesh government services "
content: THE TRIBUNE, India’s oldest, daily English-language newspaper, was first published on February 2, 1881, in Lahore (now in Pakistan), and save for 40 days in the immediate aftermath of Partition, has come out every day over the last 145 years. THE TRIBUNE was started by Sardar Dyal Singh Majithia, a public-spirited philanthropist of the time. The newspaper is run by a five-member Trust, which is chaired by Shri N N Vohra, former Governor of J&K State (2008-2018); as well as Justice S S Sodhi, former Chief Justice of the Allahabad High Court; Shri Gurbachan Jagat, former Governor of Manipur; Lt Gen. Shamsher Singh Mehta, former Western Army Commander; Shri Paramjit Singh Patwalia, Senior Advocate in the Supreme Court.THE TRIBUNE is free, objective, and independent. Restraint and moderation, rather than agitational language, are the hallmarks of the paper.The Tribune has two sister publications, Punjabi Tribune (in Punjabi) and Dainik Tribune (in Hindi).

headline: Himachal Assembly in session: House passes promotion Bill amid Opposition din
content: The Himachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly on Friday passed the Himachal Pradesh Government Services (Qualifying Experience and Regulation of Promotion) Bill, 2026, by voice vote amid a heated debate, with the House rejecting all Opposition amendments.Introduced by Chief Minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu, the Bill establishes a statutory framework for determining qualifying experience for promotions across 28 specified posts in departments including Public Works, Jal Shakti, School Education and Secretariat Administration.The legislation retrospectively amends Recruitment and Promotion Rules with effect from December 12, 2003, replacing the requirement of "length of service" in a feeder category with "qualifying experience". It empowers the state government to prescribe different experience requirements for various posts and mandates a review of Departmental Promotion Committee (DPC) proceedings conducted since December 2003 wherever revisions in seniority materially affect promotion eligibility.Opposing the Bill, BJP MLA Randhir Sharma termed it anti-employee and demanded its withdrawal or referral to a Select Committee. He alleged that the government had introduced the legislation to circumvent High Court and Supreme Court judgments granting contractual employees seniority and promotional benefits from their initial dates of appointment.Sharma argued that leaving the definition and calculation of qualifying experience to future government rules would create uncertainty, stall promotions and trigger extensive litigation.Leader of Opposition Jai Ram Thakur accused the government of attempting to defer substantial financial liabilities to the next dispensation by creating confusion over employees' service benefits. He cautioned that hastily drafted legislation without adequate legal scrutiny could expose the government and the Assembly to embarrassment if courts struck it down.BJP MLA Trilok Jamwal also opposed the proposed retrospective review, arguing that reopening nearly 23 years of DPC proceedings would open a "Pandora's box" and unsettle promotions that had already been finalised.Defending the legislation, Sukhu said it had been enacted under Article 309 of the Constitution to protect regular employees from demotion when contractual service periods were counted towards seniority. He clarified that existing promotions would remain protected until the review DPCs completed their proceedings.The Assembly also passed five other Bills: the Himachal Pradesh Sukhashray (Social Security of Women and Children of the State) Bill, 2026; the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement (Himachal Pradesh Amendment) Bill; the Himachal Pradesh Land Revenue (Amendment) Bill; the Himachal Pradesh Panchayati Raj (Third Amendment) Bill; and the Himachal Pradesh Technical Universities (Amendment) Bill.

headline: Himachal CM Sukhu inaugurates Rs 11.50-crore hospital building in Shahpur
content: Chief Minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu on Friday inaugurated the newly constructed building of the 100-bed Civil Hospital at Shahpur in Kangra district. The building has been constructed at a cost of Rs 11.50 crore.Addressing a gathering, the Chief Minister said the state government was committed to strengthening healthcare infrastructure and improving the availability of medical staff in government health institutions.He said while only 35 per cent of the sanctioned staff was available in health institutions during the previous BJP government, the present government had raised the availability of doctors, nurses, paramedical and technical staff to nearly 70 per cent.Sukhu said recruitment was being prioritised to further strengthen healthcare services. About 400 posts of doctors had already been filled and more Assistant Staff Nurses would be appointed shortly. Recruitment of Assistant Professors, Associate Professors and Professors in government medical colleges was also under way to improve medical education and healthcare delivery.Adarsh Health Institutions had been set up in every Assembly constituency, he said, with Medical Officers and Specialist Medical Officers deployed to provide better care closer to people’s homes. These institutions would be strengthened further to ensure quality services. The government, he added, would accelerate healthcare reforms in the coming years, focusing on infrastructure, staffing and patient care.Deputy Chief Whip Kewal Singh Pathania thanked the Chief Minister for providing Rs 11.50 crore for the hospital building. He said a police station and an Industrial Training Institute (ITI) were also being built at Shahpur with the government’s support and development works worth crores of rupees were under way in the constituency.

headline: Why health gain is less despite more expenses
content: INDIA’S latest National Health Accounts (NHA) estimates for 2023-24 offer an encouraging picture. Government health expenditure increased from Rs 1,29,778 crore in 2013-14 to Rs 4,14,196 crore, more than tripling in a decade. Out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE), the money households pay for healthcare, declined from 64.2% to 42.7% of the total health spending. Annual government expenditure per person increased from Rs 1,042 to Rs 2,959. These are significant achievements, but the impressive financial aggregates should not be taken at face value.For one, a declining household share of national health expenditure does not necessarily mean reduced financial hardship or more affordable healthcare. That distinction deserves greater attention than celebratory headlines.Inflation is one consideration. The increase in spending is reported in nominal rupees, without adjusting for rising prices. Adjusted for inflation, the gain in purchasing power is smaller. Population growth further dilutes the significance of aggregate expenditure. More money has undoubtedly been allocated, but each additional rupee does not purchase the same amount of healthcare it did a decade earlier.More troubling is the government's spending relative to the economy. Government health expenditure fell from 1.48% of GDP in 2022-23 to 1.43% in 2023-24. The National Health Policy 2017 envisaged reaching 2.5% by 2025. India remains far from that goal. Total health expenditure, combining public and private sources, reached Rs 9.52 lakh crore, equivalent to 3.29% of GDP, well below levels in countries at comparable stages of economic development. The overall financing envelope remains inadequate for the country's healthcare needs.The declining OOPE proportion also demands methodological caution. The latest accounts continue to draw on the National Sample Survey's 75th-round health survey, conducted in 2017-18, to estimate household health spending. Expenditure patterns have evolved since the pandemic, alongside changes in treatment prices, insurance coverage and care-seeking behaviour. Extrapolating older survey information introduces uncertainty into claims about present affordability.Lower household spending may indicate better financial protection, but it can also conceal unmet needs. A family that postpones surgery, abandons treatment or never consults a doctor because of unaffordable costs records little or no expenditure. Statistical savings can therefore coexist with suffering.The government's methodological defence deserves acknowledgment. National health accounts combine survey evidence with administrative and updated sources, while newer household expenditure surveys offer opportunities for cross-checking. Nevertheless, until recent, detailed health spending data are fully incorporated, any categorical claim that treatment has become substantially affordable is premature.Where the money goes matters as much as how much is spent. In 2023-24, around 46% of current health expenditure went towards primary care. However, the government share allocated to primary care was approximately 51%, considerably below the National Health Policy's aspiration of directing at least two-thirds of public health resources towards it. These measures have different denominators, but together they demonstrate why investment priorities warrant scrutiny.Strong primary healthcare provides prevention, early diagnosis, routine consultations and sustained management of common illnesses. This reduces avoidable complications and dependence on expensive hospital treatment. Without accessible neighbourhood clinics, reliable family physicians, medicines and diagnostics, people often enter the system only when illness becomes serious.Meanwhile, private hospitals accounted for 31.9% of current health expenditure, compared with 16.8% for government hospitals. Pharmaceutical expenditure represented 30.2%. These figures do not prove waste or unnecessary treatment. They nevertheless reveal the financial weight of hospitals and medicines within an increasingly treatment-oriented system.This imbalance matters because diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular diseases require lifelong monitoring and continuous care. Expanding hospitals without strengthening primary care risks making healthcare more technologically sophisticated but not necessarily more affordable.Insurance expansion illustrates the same contradiction. Social security expenditure on health increased from approximately 6% to 11% of total health expenditure over the decade. Private health insurance spending rose from 3.4% to 10.2%. Publicly financed schemes, particularly Ayushman Bharat, have helped eligible households access hospital treatment.Yet insurance cards do not automatically translate into financial security. A 2026 BMJ Open study involving 302,086 households found that publicly financed insurance was associated with lower out-of-pocket and catastrophic health spending. Nevertheless, protection remained incomplete, particularly for outpatient care. Consultations, medicines and tests impose recurring expenses that hospital-focused insurance schemes do not adequately address.Rising medical prices aggravate these shortcomings. Aon, a global professional services and insurance advisory firm, projected an 11.5% increase in India's employer-sponsored medical plan costs for 2026, compared with general inflation of 4.1%. Its subsequent outlook projects 10.1% medical cost growth in 2027. These insurance-related projections do not measure overall healthcare inflation but underscore persistent pricing pressure.Geographical disparities are revealing. State governments accounted for 67.9% of government health expenditure, against the Union government's 32.1%. Yet fiscal capacity, infrastructure and service delivery vary enormously. Government expenditure per person was ?1,991 in Punjab, ?3,051 in Haryana and ?5,171 in Himachal Pradesh. In Punjab, households directly financed 60.7% of total health expenditure, well above the national average.Such inequalities demand more equitable, needs-based fiscal transfers and stronger accountability for results. The Finance Commission and governments must recognise that equal allocations cannot overcome unequal starting conditions. Money must translate into available professionals, functioning facilities, essential supplies and dependable treatment.India therefore needs a measurable change in priorities: progressively achieve public spending of 2.5% of GDP, strengthen comprehensive primary care, ensure affordable medicines and diagnostics, improve transparency in private hospital pricing and extend financial protection to outpatient services. Independent evaluations should measure treatment quality, forgone care, catastrophic expenditure and the actual burden on households, rather than merely counting infrastructure and insurance enrolments.Progress should not be dismissed. Increased public spending and declining direct-payment shares are welcome developments. But these are intermediate indicators, not the outcomes citizens experience. The true test is whether an ordinary family can obtain timely, appropriate and continuous healthcare without selling assets, borrowing money or sacrificing essential consumption. Future National Health Accounts, informed by fresher household health surveys, should help answer that question more convincingly.India must move beyond celebrating expenditure towards demonstrating impact of financing. The purpose of health financing is not to make government accounts look reassuring, but to make healthcare accessible, reliable and affordable.

headline: PM Modi praises Yogi-led UP for improved security, industrial growth and development
content: LUCKNOW: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday drew a sharp contrast between Uttar Pradesh under previous governments and the BJP-led dispensation, saying the state’s public discourse had shifted from corruption and lawlessness to investor confidence, improved policing and development under Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath.He also sought to dispel concerns over Artificial Intelligence (AI) replacing jobs, asserting that skilled workers would continue to find opportunities as India moves towards becoming a developed nation by 2047.Addressing the fifth Skill Development Convocation and a ceremony honouring 52 national toppers from Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs), National Skill Training Institutes (NSTIs) and private training institutions in Lucknow, Modi praised the improvement in law and order under Yogi Adityanath, recalling a time when women found it difficult to venture out after sunset.“Today, it becomes a matter of satisfaction and pride for me when a daughter in Kashi tells me that after her duty in a factory, she can return home alone securely during the late evening hours without fear. Under Yogi ji's leadership, the BJP government has created an environment of safety here. The entire sky lies open before the youth today. Dream big, develop your skills and give it your all. Never feel that you are alone. Whenever you feel alone, just remember that I am standing with you,” the PM said.Before the event, Modi spoke to Yogi Adityanath, who reached Lucknow in the afternoon after performing the last rites of his mother, Savitri Devi, in Haridwar earlier in the day.Reflecting on Uttar Pradesh’s governance and development over the past decade, Modi said the Yogi government had instilled renewed confidence in governance and taken the state to new heights of growth and development. He cited the expanding network of expressways, the BrahMos missile manufacturing facility in Lucknow, mobile phone manufacturing and assembly, and the growing prospects of spiritual tourism.“UP has so many airports, major universities are being built and tourism is flourishing. A chip manufacturing factory is also coming up. The BrahMos missiles, which kept the enemy on edge during Operation Sindoor, are also being manufactured in UP,” he said.Describing skill development as a key pillar of his government's development strategy, Modi said a separate Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship was created after 2014 and vocational training had also been accorded prominence under the National Education Policy.Dismissing fears that AI could render millions jobless, the Prime Minister said the technological revolution would not threaten skilled workers, arguing that demand for trained manpower would only increase as India progresses towards becoming a developed nation by 2047.Referring to his economic predictions that he said had proved correct, Modi recalled being mocked when he urged people in Parliament in 2023 to invest in public sector undertakings (PSUs). “Those who followed that advice are ‘malamaal’ (prosperous) today,” he remarked.He also recalled advising people against buying gold for a year amid global economic uncertainty, claiming that those who heeded his advice had benefited from the subsequent fall in gold prices.Modi said the world was increasingly recognising the value of skill-based professions and predicted that skilled workers would command greater respect and opportunities in the years ahead.He underscored that India’s development ambitions would require a vast pool of technically trained youth capable of driving manufacturing, infrastructure expansion and emerging industries.“The country is heading towards becoming the ‘capital of skilled manpower globally. The royal families of Saudi Arabia, UAE, and others acknowledge that urban infrastructural development and their glittering cities like Dubai and Abu Dhabi are the reflection of the talent of India’s skilled workforce,” he said.Highlighting his government's record on skill development, Modi said nearly 5,000 new ITIs had been established since 2014, expanding training capacity by around five lakh seats. He also pointed to rising participation of women in vocational education, saying the number of female trainees had increased 2.5 times during the period.The Prime Minister announced that India would host the World Skills Asia Competition in Greater Noida in 2027, a move expected to strengthen Uttar Pradesh’s profile as a hub for technical education and skill development.Modi also criticised previous governments and colonial-era policies for fostering a mindset that glorified white-collar jobs while undervaluing vocational skills. He said India had historically been known for its specialised crafts and skilled artisans, but invaders had targeted its skilled industries and craftsmen to weaken its economic strength.“When invaders came, they first targeted India’s skilled industries and artisans because they understood that Bharat’s prosperity rested on its skills,” he said, referring to accounts of artisans being subjected to mutilation, including the chopping off of thumbs and limbs, to prevent them from reproducing their craftsmanship..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

headline: KTR Condemns Attack On Meta Office
content: HYDERABAD: BRS working president K.T. Rama Rao condemned the attack by Youth Congress activists on the Meta office in Gachibowli. He recalled that ‘Brand Hyderabad’ was built over many years through hard work and industry-friendly policies and expressed serious concern over the conduct of Congress activists. In a post on his ‘X’ handle, Rama Rao said Friday’s incident did not merely break the glass at Meta’s office but also damaged the trust and credibility that Hyderabad had painstakingly built among global investors over several decades. Questioning the Congress government's record, Rama Rao asked whether it had managed to bring even one major international brand like Meta to Hyderabad during its three years in power. “Rahul Gandhi, is goondaism your way of bringing companies to India? In three years of your party’s governance in Telangana, have you brought even ONE major global brand like Meta to Hyderabad? Has your party now launched a new model of attracting companies through goondaism, even in a state where it is in power?” Rama Rao posted.

headline: Record Turnout Marks Ladakh’s First Grassroots Polls As UT
content: SRINAGAR: Ladakh on Saturday witnessed an overwhelming voter turnout in its first Panchayat and Municipal Council elections since becoming a Union Territory in 2019, with residents braving challenging terrain and weather conditions to participate in what many described as a landmark exercise in grassroots democracy. According to official figures, the Union Territory recorded 73.60 per cent polling for Panchayat elections, including 70.03 per cent voting for Sarpanch posts, while 52.40 per cent turnout was registered in Municipal Council polls. The elections, the first local-body polls in Ladakh since 2018 and the first after the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir was reorganised in August 2019, were hailed by Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena as a historic milestone in the region's democratic journey. In a message posted on 'X', the Lt Governor expressed gratitude to the people of Ladakh for their enthusiastic participation, noting that the Panchayat turnout had surpassed the 67.8 per cent overall turnout recorded in the 2018 Panchayat elections. “Heartfelt gratitude to the resilient people of the Union Territory of Ladakh for coming out in overwhelming numbers to cast their votes in the Panchayat and Municipal elections. Today's voter turnout, with 73.60 percent polling for Panch and 70.03 percent for Sarpanch, marks an improvement over the overall voter turnout of 67.8 percent recorded in the 2018 Panchayat elections, reflecting an encouraging level of public participation in the democratic process and celebrating the true essence of democracy,” he said. Saxena described the participation of voters across age groups, from first-time electors to senior citizens, as a powerful demonstration of public faith in democratic institutions and local self-governance. He said the elections represented a “proud milestone” in strengthening grassroots democracy and thanked Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah for their commitment to empowering local governance in Ladakh. Reports from across Ladakh indicated a vibrant polling atmosphere as young voters, women, senior citizens, monks and community leaders queued up at polling stations to exercise their democratic right. The elections were conducted across some of India's most remote and strategically significant border regions. The Panchayat elections covered 192 Panchayat Halqas across eight districts, involving 192 Sarpanch posts and 1,428 Panch seats. Of these, 55 Sarpanches and 1,186 Panches were elected unopposed, leaving 137 Sarpanch and 242 Panch seats to be decided through voting. Municipal Council elections were held for 38 wards, including 21 wards in Leh and 17 in Kargil. Polling took place in all 21 wards of Leh, while in Kargil four wards were filled unopposed and voting was conducted in the remaining 13 wards. Election authorities made extensive logistical arrangements to ensure smooth polling in the mountainous region. In the remote Zanskar valley, helicopter services were deployed to transport polling personnel and election material to three polling stations that remain inaccessible by road. Officials, security personnel and local administration teams worked in coordination to facilitate voting across geographically challenging areas. While the high turnout underscored public participation in the electoral process, the polling day also unfolded against the backdrop of ongoing protests by sections of Ladakh's civil society seeking greater democratic safeguards and constitutional protections. At a press conference in Leh on Saturday, climate activist Sonam Wangchuk, alongside leaders of the Leh Apex Body (LAB), reiterated that they were not opposed to elections but were advocating for broader democratic representation and genuine participation in decision-making processes. LAB chairman Chhering Dorjey Lakruk said the people of Ladakh support democratic processes but believe elections alone do not address long-standing concerns regarding governance, representation and the region's political future. He also questioned the timing of upcoming Hill Council elections during winter, arguing that many Ladakhis move outside the region during the harsh season, potentially affecting voter participation. “People are not against elections. Elections should be held when people are present in their homes and can participate in the democratic process without difficulty,” Lakruk said. Wangchuk raised concerns about alleged omissions from electoral rolls and asserted that Ladakh's people were seeking democratic rights and institutions comparable to those available elsewhere in the country. Addressing the press alongside LAB leaders, he criticised what he described as decision-making without adequate local consultation and urged the Centre to take note of the concerns being voiced by residents. headline: High turnout, voter deletions, and a brewing political contest in Ladakh
content: Panchayat and Urban Local Body polls in Ladakh concluded Saturday with 70.03 percent turnout in Panchayat elections and 52.40 percent in municipal polls. The administration said this marked an improvement over the overall voter turnout of 67.8 percent recorded in the 2018 Panchayat elections. Lieutenant Governor V K Saxena said the turnout reflected "an encouraging level of public participation in the democratic process and celebrates the true essence of democracy.” He added that witnessing everyone, “from the enthusiastic first-time voters to our respected senior citizens,” was a “powerful testament to people’s unshakeable faith” in the democratic process and local self-governance. He also stated that these were the first Panchayat and municipal elections since 2018 and the first since Ladakh was made a Union Territory in 2019, adding that “it marks a proud milestone in self-governance”. As per official figures, there are 192 panchayats in Ladakh. Of these, 55 have elected their sarpanches unopposed. There are also 1,428 panch constituencies, of which 1,186 have been declared elected uncontested, while about 212 panchs are yet to be elected. Meanwhile, climate activist Sonam Wangchuk and Apex Body Leh chairman Dorjay Lakrook alleged that “several voters faced deletions” in Saturday’s election, especially young voters who were not included in the voters' list. Wangchuk also claimed he had been placed under house arrest, with security personnel deployed outside his residence, and was not allowed to step out even when he tried. The activist marked his presence at the ongoing protest in Leh after the police deployment outside his residence was removed. Ladakh Police said in a post on Saturday that ADM Leh had passed a “prohibitory order” against Sonam Wangchuk and sought to clarify that he had not been placed under house arrest. Hitting out at the Lieutenant Governor V K Saxena-led administration again, Wangchuk reiterated the demand to delay hill council polls scheduled for December 4. He also urged the Centre to reconsider the polls, alleging that the decision to push through elections despite the people's opposition was aimed at “derail[ing] the ongoing talks” between the Ministry of Home Affairs and Ladakhi socio-political representatives. “In the short term, the local administration may think that this will benefit them, but in the long term, the country will have to bear a national security cost. The prime minister and the whole country need to view this as a national security concern,” Wangchuk said. Wangchuk stated that the government was upsetting people in a sensitive border region and “the Ministry of Defence should be more concerned about this because Ladakh has always supported them in previous wars and this sentiment should stay the same in the future. I believe that is bigger than the MHA, and the MoD should consider whether this is in favour of the country’s Security. Why are such patriotic people being distressed?” He added that never in the history of the hill councils had elections been conducted in December. “We are not against any election, but forced elections without including the local people - how does that help bring faith in elected representatives?” Meanwhile, Apex Body chairman Lakrook underlined that the basic principle of any election was maximum participation, “which is defeated by holding polling in this temperature in Ladakh,” citing the migration of a large part of the population from Ladakh to warmer regions.

content: Hyderabad: BRS official spokesperson Manne Krishank strongly condemned the attack by Congress cadres on Meta’s office in Gachibowli, calling it a deplorable act.In a statement on Saturday Krishank said it was a matter of pride for Telangana that the world’s second-largest Meta campus was established in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, during the KCR govt. headline: SEBI Urges Directors To Challenge Management, IRDAI Seeks Human Oversight Of AI
content: Mumbai: Independent judgement in company boardrooms and human oversight of artificial intelligence took centre stage as the 11th Gatekeepers of Governance summit opened on Thursday at the Trident Hotel in Nariman Point. Organised by Excellence Enablers, chaired by former SEBI chairman M Damodaran, the two-day event brought together regulators, directors, executives and investors to discuss how boards can hold management to account and retain human control over critical decisions as businesses adopt AI.Opening the summit with a discussion on whether regulation can keep pace with changes in business, SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said independent directors must demonstrate their independence through the decisions they take. Eligibility criteria and appointment procedures set the terms for joining a board, he said. Effective oversight depends on directors exercising their own judgement, questioning management constructively and taking an active part in deliberations.Pandey outlined SEBI’s efforts to make compliance more proportionate for listed companies while strengthening accountability and investor protection. The work includes using quantitative thresholds to assess whether an event is material, reviewing requirements for related-party transactions and tailoring disclosures to the nature and significance of those transactions. The regulator is also exploring ways to help independent directors build the expertise needed to scrutinise increasingly complex businesses.SEBI has separately issued a consultation paper on how companies use of funds raised through public issues should be monitored. It proposes allowing monitoring agencies to submit their reports directly to stock exchanges and extending monitoring requirements to public issues regardless of size. Another proposal would review how exchanges penalise listed companies for non-compliance, with the aim of preventing multiple penalties for the same violation. Attendance At Board Meetings Improved In Maharatna, Navratna Cos: Excellence EnablersOn sustainability reporting, the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation are required to make structured environmental, social and governance disclosures under the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting framework. Pandey said SEBI was working to make value-chain disclosures more practical by limiting the scope of those requirements to significant business partners.The question of who exercises judgement became especially pressing as the discussion turned to artificial intelligence. Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) Chairman Ajay Seth said nearly 85% of Indian insurers use AI in some form, including in underwriting and claims. He urged insurers to train their models for Indian conditions and keep people in control of critical decisions. A separate panel examined what company directors should continue to scrutinise as businesses rely more heavily on automated tools.Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) Chairman S Ramann said the regulator was examining whether elements of the Unified Pension Scheme (UPS) could be adapted to offer private-sector employees more predictable retirement income. The UPS combines the National Pension System framework with a defined-benefit component backed by actuarial calculations and a government-backed liability structure. Ramann said discussions with the insurance regulator were exploring whether a market-based mechanism could provide pension guarantees. Paytm Advisory Panel Discussing Terms Of Reference With Company: Damodaran Guarantees carry costs that would need careful assessment, Ramann said, adding that such a model would have to be developed in phases. He noted that some subscribers had chosen to keep their individual National Pension System accounts during the transition to the UPS, citing the investment returns they had earned and their willingness to manage their own retirement savings. As longer life expectancy raises the risk of people outliving those savings, he called for pension products suited to different income groups and wider distribution through banks and other financial institutions.The summit also considered how nomination and remuneration committees should prepare for both planned leadership transitions and unexpected departures. A session on the National Financial Reporting Authority was scheduled to examine how audit oversight can curb aggressive accounting and help ensure financial statements fairly reflect a company’s position. Taking Stakeholders For A RidePanellists examined how parent companies oversee their subsidiaries and whether changes to corporate group structures could strengthen accountability. A separate discussion focused on governance practices at start-ups. Speakers at the summit included State Bank of India Chairman CS Setty, Crisil Managing Director and Chief Executive Amish Mehta, and former SEBI whole-time members Amarjeet Singh and G Ananth Narayan.Level up your brain the fun way. headline: Pakistani minister gets clearance for Taj Mahal visit, denied Nizamuddin Dargah trip
content: HYDERABAD: Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Masood Malik has been granted permission to visit the Taj Mahal in Agra but denied clearance for a proposed visit to the Hazrat Nizamuddin Dargah in Delhi during his ongoing trip to India.Malik is in New Delhi to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum, being held from November 20 to 22..The Pakistan High Commission had sought permission for the minister to visit several locations, including the Taj Mahal, Humayun's Tomb, Dilli Haat and the Nizamuddin Dargah. While authorities approved visits to the other sites, security agencies did not clear the proposed trip to the shrine.The visit marks the first trip by a Pakistani federal minister to India since former foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari attended the SCO foreign ministers' meeting in Goa in May 2023.(With inputs from agencies)

headline: India’s space race needs balance, not just speed | Hindustan Times
content: India's space story is entering a new and important phase. From a programme once dominated almost entirely by the government, the country is moving towards a much broader ecosystem involving ISRO, public-sector enterprises, start-ups, established companies, telecom operators, technology firms and international partners.There are now roughly 440 Indian space start-ups, private investment has crossed $618 million and the country's space economy is estimated at around $9 billion. The ambition is considerably larger: India hopes to build a $40-45 billion space economy over the coming decade.But there is a danger hidden beneath these impressive numbers. India may be increasing capacity faster than it is creating balance. A space economy is not a collection of independent industries. It is a chain. A customer creates demand for a service; that service requires a satellite; the satellite requires spectrum and orbital permissions; it has to be manufactured, launched and controlled; its data must reach ground stations, cloud and computing networks; and finally, the service must reach a paying user.If one link is missing, the entire chain is weakened. That means the more important question for India is not: How many satellites can we build? It is: How many satellites can we economically manufacture, authorise, launch, operate, connect to the ground and sell services from? That is a very different measure of space power.India has made considerable progress in launch technology. PSLV, GSLV, LVM3 and SSLV provide a strong foundation, while new launch infrastructure is being developed at Sriharikota and Kulasekarapattinam. Private launch companies are also emerging. But launch capacity is not simply a question of the number of rockets or launch pads.A rocket may be available, but not at the required price, on the required date, or for the required orbit. Engines, suppliers, testing facilities, range availability, payload readiness and launch scheduling can all become bottlenecks.The same applies to satellite manufacturing. The commercial space age is moving away from building a handful of large, bespoke satellites towards producing constellations of standardised spacecraft. That requires factories, common satellite platforms, modular payloads, automated testing and reliable supplies of space-grade electronics, sensors, propulsion systems and other components. India is moving in this direction, but its industrial capacity is still fragmented. There is also a danger of creating manufacturing capacity before sufficient customers exist. The opposite danger is equally real: demand may grow rapidly while India lacks the components and high-volume production capacity needed to meet it. The answer is, therefore, not simply more capacity. It is better synchronised capacity.Perhaps the least measured part of India's space economy is customer demand. Government agencies alone can generate enormous requirements—communications, Earth observation, defence, navigation, disaster management, meteorology, agriculture and maritime surveillance. The commercial market adds broadband, enterprise connectivity, aviation, maritime services, IoT, mapping, logistics, financial services and climate intelligence.Yet demand remains fragmented. Government could play a particularly important role by becoming an anchor customer, but this requires aggregation of requirements across ministries and departments. NSIL already has a role in aggregating demand and commercialising space services. That role should be strengthened.Instead of every department thinking about buying a satellite, government should increasingly think about buying an outcome. Why purchase a satellite when what is really required is persistent imagery? Why purchase communications hardware when what is required is secure connectivity? Why purchase a spacecraft when what is required is intelligence?This points towards a new model: Space-as-a-Service—EO-as-a-Service, ISR-as-a-Service, PNT-as-a-Service, Satcom-as-a-Service and Space Domain Awareness-as-a-Service. Such a model could provide industry with predictable demand while allowing government to purchase capability rather than hardware.There is another constraint that is easy to overlook because it is largely invisible: spectrum. A company can have the money, the satellite, the rocket and the customer—and still be unable to provide the service if spectrum coordination and national authorisation are not ready.This is particularly important as India moves towards LEO broadband, direct-to-device services, mobile satellite services and large NGSO constellations. The issue is not simply that the world is "running out" of spectrum. The larger challenge is coordination, interference management, orbital resources and predictable access. Spectrum must therefore be treated as an industrial input, alongside land, power and capital.A company planning a constellation should know at the beginning—not near the end of the programme—what frequencies it will need, what ITU coordination will be required, what national permissions are necessary and what ground infrastructure will be needed. The emerging regulatory framework is an important step forward. But regulation itself has now become part of industrial capacity.India has traditionally thought of space in terms of rockets and satellites. The commercial constellation era will force a different mindset. Every satellite needs a ground architecture. That means gateways, antenna farms, telemetry and control stations, mission-control centres, fibre networks, cloud infrastructure, data centres, cybersecurity, edge computing and AI-enabled data processing.A satellite without its ground infrastructure is little more than an isolated spacecraft. India already possesses substantial government ground infrastructure. But hundreds or thousands of commercial satellites will require a much more distributed architecture.The future will increasingly look like: Satellite → Gateway → Fibre → Cloud → AI → Edge → User. Ground infrastructure must therefore be developed alongside, and in some cases ahead of, satellite constellations.There is also a strong case for shared commercial infrastructure. Instead of every operator building its own gateway, antenna farm and mission-control infrastructure, India could create a national commercial ground infrastructure grid, allowing multiple operators to share expensive facilities. That would reduce costs and improve utilisation.The emerging picture is revealing. India is relatively strong in launch technology and mission engineering. Satellite manufacturing is expanding rapidly. Data-centre capacity is growing. Start-up investment is increasing.But customer aggregation remains uncertain. Spectrum coordination is becoming more demanding. Ground infrastructure will have to scale dramatically. Critical components remain a concern. Skills in systems engineering, mission operations, spectrum management and space data are still developing. Above all, there is an integration deficit. This is perhaps the most important conclusion for policymakers.India could build more rockets than its satellites require. It could build more satellites than customers can buy. Customers could sign contracts before spectrum is available. Spectrum could be available before gateways are constructed.Satellites could be launched before adequate ground infrastructure exists. Data could be generated faster than it can be processed. Each segment may look successful individually while the overall ecosystem remains inefficient.The solution should not be greater government control over industry. It should be greater visibility across the ecosystem. India should establish a National Space Capacity Dashboard, updated periodically and bringing together information on satellite production, launch capacity, launch slots, spectrum filings, orbital resources, ground stations, gateways, data-processing capacity, government demand and commercial contracts.The country should also develop a five-, 10- and 15-year national satellite demand register so that industry can see where future demand is likely to emerge. A Space Capacity Bank could go a step further by matching unused launch capacity, manufacturing capacity, ground-station time and data-processing resources with companies that need them.This would allow India to extract more value from existing infrastructure before investing in additional capacity. The objective should be neither maximum capacity nor minimum capacity. It should be optimal capacity with strategic reserves.An industry operating permanently at 100% capacity has no resilience when a launch fails, a supplier collapses or demand suddenly surges. Equally, chronically underutilised infrastructure represents wasted capital.By 2030, India's space sector should be judged not by how many rockets it launches or how many satellites it builds, but by whether the complete chain works. Customers should have a visible pipeline.Manufacturers should be capable of producing spacecraft at industrial scale. Launchers should provide reliable and affordable access to orbit, while foreign launchers remain available as a resilience mechanism.Spectrum and orbital coordination should begin before satellites enter production. Ground infrastructure should grow alongside constellations. Satellite data should flow seamlessly into cloud, AI, GIS and edge-computing systems. And the country should have enough engineers, spectrum specialists, orbital analysts, mission operators, cybersecurity professionals and space-data scientists to operate the system.The ultimate measure should be simple: How much usable, revenue-generating and strategically valuable space capability can India deliver every year? That is a far better measure of a space power than the number of rockets, satellites or start-ups.India has already demonstrated that it can build a space ecosystem. The next challenge is to make that ecosystem work as one integrated system. The space race is no longer only about reaching orbit. It is about creating an economically viable, technologically resilient and strategically secure chain from the customer on Earth to the satellite in space—and back again.India's ambition should, therefore, not be to build the maximum number of rockets or satellites. It should be to build the right capacity, in the right place, at the right time, connected to the right customer. That is how a space programme becomes a space power.(The views expressed are personal)This article is authored by Lt Gen PJS Pannu, former deputy chief, IDS, founder, Space Club of India, chief mentor, Department of Space Studies, MERI and senior advisor, Space Industries Association.

headline: Ladakh records 70% turnout in first panchayat polls since Union Territory formation
content: Leh/Kargil Ladakh recorded 70.03% turnout in the panchayat elections and 52.4% in the municipal council polls on Saturday (November 21, 2026), even as the Leh Apex Body (LAB), a civil society body holding talks with the Union Home Ministry, expressed unhappiness over the electoral process and flagged several issues, including fears of voter deletion, and questioned the timing of the polls while discussions were being held on Statehood and the Sixth Schedule. Also read | Ladakh hill council polls: 541 candidates file nominations https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/ladakh/ladakh-hill-council-polls-541-candidates-file-nominations/article71713482.ece A spokesperson of the Ladakh administration said the region witnessed an “overwhelming voter turnout in its first panchayat and municipal council elections”, since it was formed as a Union Territory in 2019 from the erstwhile State of Jammu and Kashmir. https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/jammu-and-kashmir/ “With 70.03% turnout in panchayat elections and 52.4% in municipal elections, the enthusiastic participation reflects the people’s deep commitment to grassroots democracy and local self-governance,” the spokesperson said. Highlighting the tough topography of the cold desert mountain region, officials said helicopter services were deployed to airlift polling teams to three remote and road-inaccessible polling stations in Zanskar. Ladakh announces hill council elections, but fails to assuage protesting civil society groups Ladakh announces hill council elections, but fails to assuage protesting civil society groups Hill council seats increased to 100, with 36 reserved for women for the first time; civil society groups oppose unilateral decision to hold polls now despite concerns about delimitation, voting in winter Ladakh announces hill council elections, but fails to assuage protesting civil society groups storyline 1 Many first-time voters expressed satisfaction over the process. “I felt good casting my vote for the first time to elect a representative,” said Kaneez Fatima, a voter from Chushot. Many voters, like Stanzin Padma, covered large distances from the Leh town to cast their vote. “I travelled from Leh city to Temisgam village, 92 km away, to exercise my franchise,” Ms. Padma said. The Ladakh administration said these elections “mark an important step towards providing representative platforms for addressing local development priorities, civic amenities and public services.” “The people of Ladakh have expressed their conviction through the ballot. The overwhelming participation in the first local-body elections since the formation of the Union Territory marks a significant milestone in Ladakh’s democratic journey, laying a strong foundation for democratic decentralisation, representative institutions, participatory governance and accountable local self-government,” the administration official said. ‘Historic day’ Lieutenant-Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena termed the elections as “a historic day for Ladakh”. “Today’s voter turnout, with 73.6% polling for Panch and 70.03% for Sarpanch, marks an improvement over the overall voter turnout of 67.8% recorded in the 2018 Panchayat elections. This reflects an encouraging level of public participation in the democratic process and celebrating the true essence of democracy,” Mr. Saxena said. “Witnessing everyone, from the enthusiastic first-time voters to our respected senior citizens, is a powerful testament to people’s unshakeable faith in the democratic process and local self-governance,” he added. The Lieutenant-Governor said this was the first Panchayat and municipal elections since 2018, and the first time since Ladakh was made a UT in 2019, marking a proud milestone in self-governance. He also thanked Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah for their steadfast vision and commitment to empowering and strengthening grassroots democracy across Ladakh. The panchayat elections covered 192 panchayat halqas across eight districts, comprising 192 sarpanch positions and 1,428 panch seats. Of these, 55 sarpanches and 1,186 panches were elected unopposed. The municipal council elections covered 38 wards, comprising 21 in Leh town and 17 in Kargil town. Polling was conducted in all 21 wards of Leh, while four wards in Kargil were filled unopposed and polling was held in the remaining 13 wards, according to the spokesperson. Dissatisfied with poll process Meanwhile, climate activist Sonam Wangchuk and LAB co-chairman Tsering Dorjey Lakrook, expressed unhappiness over the process. “Participation projected is not true because 25-30% locals have moved outside Ladakh. The decision to allow voters from the 2018 rolls disallowed many Gen Z voters to participate. We also fear deletion of voters from the list. Several villages also boycotted these elections. We fear rigging like we saw in West Bengal, Bihar, etc. No Special Intensive Revision (SIR) was held in Ladakh but still there are reports of large-scale deletions,” Mr. Lakrook said. Activist Wangchuk, who spoke at the ongoing protest site of NDS Memorial Park in Leh, said, “I was let free from my residence at HIAL (Himalayan Institute of Alternatives Ladakh) after the government faced the truth in the Supreme Court on November 19. Earlier, security personnel and vehicles manning my residence were also thinned out. It’s sad the state is behaving like a rogue state.” Mr. Wangchuk was shifted from the protest site on November 11 and placed under a security cover at his HIAL residence. The Ladakh administration had also imposed restrictions on his movement for the next 60 days. “For unknown reasons, the polling booth was completely shifted from my village. Several villages boycotted these elections, with many unhappy with the delimitation process. Several parties are contesting because they fear the results will be declared based on nominations only. It’s not an inclusive election,” Mr. Wangchuk said. He reiterated the demand to postpone the December 4 hill council elections in eight districts. “A few bureaucrats from their centrally-heated offices plan these elections and do not know how it feels to stay in freezing temperature in Drass, among the coldest regions in the world, and other parts,” Mr. Wangchuk said. He sought the intervention of President Droupadi Murmu and Prime Minister Narendra Modi “to stop imposition of elections against the will of the people of Ladakh”. He said these elections were aimed at “derailing the current dialogue between the Centre and the civil society groups of Ladakh” over Statehood and Sixth Schedule. “The Centre is backtracking from its May 22 promise to have an elected body with all officials under it,” he added. Warns of national security fallout Mr. Wangchuk said the situation in the sensitive region of Ladakh “has now become a security issue and the Defence Ministry should also look into what is going on”. “There is a risk to the security of the nation. It may not make a difference during peacetime but will matter in war times. People of Ladakh have always stood with the Army during the wars, and any dissatisfaction among people is not good for the nation’s security,” Mr. Wangchuk said.

headline: Relentless Rajagopal gets call from Delhi to meet Sandeep on November 23
content: HYDERABAD: Munugode MLA Komatireddy Rajagopal Reddy continued to bait the state leadership on Friday even as he revealed that AICC secretary Sachin Sawant had asked him to make himself available for a meeting with newly appointed Telangana Congress in-charge BM Sandeep on November 23.He took to X to “advise” leaders holding high constitutional and political positions to maintain dignity in their public statements, in an apparent swipe at Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy. Later in the day, speaking exclusively to TNIE, Rajagopal Reddy ruled out leaving the Congress,The latest salvo came a day after Revanth made indirect remarks against him at a public meeting in Siddipet. Taking to X on Friday, Rajagopal Reddy cautioned those holding high constitutional and political offices against arrogance and arbitrary behaviour merely because they were in power.The MLA warned that the people of Telangana and history would not forgive rulers who misused power, indulged in corruption, neglected public needs and delivered undemocratic governance. Urging the chief minister and other senior leaders to introspect, he called for honest and ethical administration and the fulfilment of promises made to the people. He also prayed to Lord Ayyappa to bless the state’s leadership with wisdom and the ability to govern responsibly. People watching every move of leaders: MLAEarlier, speaking to reporters at his residence, Rajagopal Reddy had been more direct in his criticism of the chief minister.“People are watching what Revanth Reddy is saying. A person holding such a high position should introspect about his own words,” he said..He said the chief minister had a responsibility to protect all Congress MLAs and claimed that he had met Revanth several times to convey his concerns, but his advice had gone unheeded.“That is why I am being forced to speak out like this. Shed your arrogance and govern honestly. Do not hand over the state to thieves,” the MLA remarked.Questioning the government’s claim of providing corruption-free administration, he challenged the chief minister to introspect. “Do not speak arrogantly. Place your hand on your heart and ask yourself whether you are providing corruption-free governance,” he said.Against this backdrop, Rajagopal Reddy said he would take up his grievances with Sandeep when they meet on November 23. headline: ‘Lots of money to waste on lawyers’: Supreme Court rejects Tamil Nadu’s Cauvery water plea | India News
content: The Supreme Court on Friday dismissed Tamil Nadu’s plea seeking directions to Karnataka to immediately release an alleged backlog of over 11.7 thousand million cubic feet (TMC) of Cauvery water, with the bench remarking that the state appeared to have “lots of money to waste on lawyers” after it filed yet another application in the decades-old inter-state river dispute.A bench of justices Vikram Nath and Aparesh Kumar Singh rejected Tamil Nadu’s application seeking directions to Karnataka to clear the alleged shortfall accumulated up to October 6 by releasing 1.3 TMC of water a day for 10 days at Billigundulu, the key measuring station on the Karnataka-Tamil Nadu border.‘Lots of money to waste on lawyers’“The application is dismissed. You have filed another application today. It looks like the State of Tamil Nadu has lots of money to waste on lawyers… We have dismissed this application and we will also dismiss the other application,” said justice Nath while reading out the operative part of the order. The remark came as the bench noted that Tamil Nadu had moved another application on Friday, seeking fresh directions against Karnataka.Friday’s order denies Tamil Nadu any relief, which has repeatedly approached the Supreme Court alleging that Karnataka hasn’t released its due share of Cauvery water despite having sufficient reservoir storage, leaving farmers in the state facing water shortages. Tamil Nadu contended that Karnataka was withholding water despite having a combined reservoir storage of around 49 TMC, which it insisted was adequate to meet its obligations to the lower riparian state. It also accused the Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA) and the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee (CWRC) of failing to direct Karnataka to make good the accumulated shortfall, despite their fortnightly meetings.Opposing the plea, Karnataka argued that several districts in the state were facing drought and that its irrigation allocations had been reduced accordingly. Under the Supreme Court’s water-sharing verdict, Karnataka must release 177 TMC of Cauvery water to Tamil Nadu in a normal year, with the allocation reduced proportionately in years of distress.Tamil Nadu-Karnataka spar over Cauvery waterTamil Nadu has maintained that even after accounting for the reduced allocation in the current distress year, Karnataka still owes it a substantial quantity of water. It also argued that the lower riparian state could not bear the entire burden of deficient rainfall and hydrological distress.Reacting to the verdict, Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar said the state would have supplied Cauvery water to Tamil Nadu if it had adequate reserves, but was currently struggling to meet even its own drinking water requirements. “Yes, if we have water, we will certainly give water to Tamil Nadu. We do not have water even for drinking. I have to protect our state. I had cautioned our farmers earlier about water availability,” Shivakumar was quoted as saying by PTI.Also Read I ₹1,427-crore sand mining case">Former-Tamil Nadu minister, government officials named in ₹1,427-crore sand mining caseWhile the TN government was yet to react to the verdict, former CM MK Stalin said in a statement, “Kuruvai is gone, and Samba is withering, and farmers are struggling...and what is the CM’s answer, who is in silent mode.”
